section_summary: This section closes a report on the Second National Diet and includes lists of its legislation and a statement by General Douglas MacArthur. It then covers Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida’s address to the Fourth Diet and gives a detailed account of the Fifth Diet’s legislation, budget, party politics and debates over foreign affairs. The section ends partway through a Japanese Foreign Ministry report on the Fifth Diet.

subfiles.title: Public Comments on Accomplishments of the Second National Diet
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch compares MacArthur’s praise for the Diet’s legislative achievements with critical Japanese press coverage.
subfiles.summary: Sebald attributes the press’s failure to explain the Diet’s democratic reforms partly to inadequate press relations.

subfiles.title: Important Bills Passed During 2nd National Diet
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists 29 important laws passed by the Second National Diet.
subfiles.summary: Lists major judicial, administrative, education, economic and public health measures.

subfiles.title: Bills Not Favorably Acted Upon by 2nd National Diet
subfiles.about: The enclosure identifies Second Diet bills left in committee or withdrawn by the Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Lists 43 unsuccessful bills, separating those not reported by committee from those withdrawn by the Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Statement by General Douglas MacArthur
subfiles.about: MacArthur praises enactment of legislation implementing Japan’s constitution, especially habeas corpus.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur says the completed legislation protects individual life, liberty and dignity.

subfiles.title: Prime Minister’s Address at Opening of Fourth Session of National Diet, December 4, 1948
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sebald transmits and assesses Yoshida’s opening address to the Fourth Diet.
subfiles.summary: The despatch outlines Yoshida’s case for an election, supplementary budget and economic recovery. It reports widespread newspaper criticism that his policy speech lacked specifics.

subfiles.title: Address of the Prime Minister before the 4th Session of the National Diet
subfiles.about: Yoshida presents his government’s case for a supplementary budget, election and political reform.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida discusses public service pay, disaster relief, repatriation, fiscal restraint and education. He calls for a general election and action against corruption, linking democratic government and economic recovery to a peace settlement.

subfiles.title: The Fifth National Diet of Japan
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: The despatch reviews the Fifth Diet’s legislation, political conduct and emerging balance of power.
subfiles.summary: The Fifth Diet enacted 226 of 251 submitted bills, including a balanced budget, personnel reductions, ministry reorganization and labor law changes. Huston reviews unresolved bills, Diet investigations, resolutions, brawls and press reaction. He credits Yoshida with effective leadership while noting the House of Councillors’ growing independence and difficult issues expected at the next session.

subfiles.title: Government Personnel, Old and New
subfiles.about: The enclosure compares authorized government staffing before and after planned reductions.
subfiles.summary: The chart gives an overall reduction of 240,811 posts and estimates about 174,000 actual dismissals after vacancies are counted.

subfiles.title: Summary of Legislation, 5th National Diet, 11 February–31 May 1949
subfiles.from: Government Section, Parliamentary and Political Division
subfiles.about: The table records enacted Fifth Diet bills and their introduction and passage dates.
subfiles.summary: The table reports 251 bills introduced and 226 enacted, then lists the enacted measures by sponsoring house or ministry. It covers public administration, budgets, trade, transport, education, labor, health and other fields, with dates for action in both Diet houses.

subfiles.title: Legislative Summary, 11 February–31 May 1949
subfiles.from: Government Section, Parliamentary and Political Division
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists the 25 bills that did not pass the Fifth Diet.
subfiles.summary: Lists unsuccessful bills and marks those referred to interim committees.

subfiles.title: Tokyo’s Despatch No. 378 of June 13, 1949
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum condenses the Fifth Diet despatch for departmental use.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes budget and personnel legislation, favorable press reaction, Yoshida’s strengthened position and issues expected at another session.

subfiles.title: Review of Fifth Special Session of the Diet
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards a Japanese Foreign Ministry report on the Fifth Diet’s foreign affairs debates.
subfiles.summary: The despatch highlights debate over peace, neutrality, foreign trade and repatriation, alongside the Diet’s polarized party politics.

subfiles.title: Report on the Proceedings of the Fifth Special Diet Session
subfiles.about: The report analyzes Fifth Diet proceedings, especially matters affecting the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: The report’s opening sections cover Diet interest in a peace treaty, security, neutrality and foreign trade, then trace debates over the respective trade responsibilities of the Foreign Ministry and the Ministry of International Trade and Industry. It reviews disputes over the budget, taxes, unemployment and the influence of Dodge’s economic program. The section ends during its account of the new Investigation Special Committee and opposition to its proposed remit.
